entry.evidence: The identification of their parental material is crucial to understand rheological contrasts and related ductile deformation in the Rotondo granite.

steps.action: Posed two open questions from the literature: what the parent material of the dark shear zones (classified as sheared lamprophyres) is, and when the ductile deformation and foliation formed.
steps.quote: although the mineralogical composition questions their interpretation as former mafic dykes

steps.action: Summarized the published Alpine deformation stages (D1 to D4) and their expected kinematics and timing for the Gotthard massif, later used as the rival framework for the shear zones.
steps.quote: The Alpine tectonic evolution of the Central Alps has been intensely studied

steps.action: Adopted the existing tunnel section of Schneider (1985) for foliation and fault-zone orientations and petrology along the tunnel.
steps.quote: The orientation data of the foliation and fault zones are mainly adopted from the existing tunnel section of Schneider (70)

steps.action: Mapped and sampled the tunnel (30 samples): Tremola and Prato series, equigranular (RG1) and porphyritic (RG2) granite varieties, foliation continuing into aplitic dykes, magmatic and sharp-contact enclaves, and granitic versus quartz-biotite-rich shear zones with their orientations and top-to-south reverse shear sense.
steps.quote: Petrology, microstructures, and kinematics of 30 representative samples were studied

steps.action: Checked shear direction from boudin/swell axes against biotite lineations and checked the shear sense against the contacts of the Prato series with the Tremola series and the Rotondo granite.
steps.quote: The latter indicate the shear direction and correspond well with the biotite lineations.

steps.action: Measured 2D grain sizes of magmatic and dynamically recrystallized quartz in RG1, RG2 and G-SZ samples by optical microscopy, estimating mean grain sizes of coarse- and fine-grained domains.
steps.quote: Grain sizes of 80 to 121 grains per sample were measured.

steps.action: Selected zircons from one RG1, one RG2 and one QB-SZ sample to test the intrusion age, compare the two varieties, and identify the QB-SZ parent material.
steps.quote: zircons of a QB-SZ (sample B20-2801) were examined to obtain indications of the parent material of the deformed rocks

steps.action: Corrected LA-ICP-MS U–Th–Pb data with the GJ-1 primary standard and controlled ages with secondary zircon reference materials; calibrated trace elements on NIST-610.
steps.quote: A quality control of the resulting ages was carried out by using secondary reference materials

steps.action: Derived the RG1 206Pb/238U age range (285–319 Ma, peak ~295 Ma, mean 296.1 ± 3.6 Ma, MSWD 7.07) after discarding discordant data and Chauvenet outliers.
steps.quote: have a range of 285–319 Ma with a distinct peak at

steps.action: Used the near-unity MSWD of the secondary reference materials to rule out underestimated analytical uncertainty as the cause of the high sample MSWD.
steps.quote: The latter attribution is rather unlikely, since the MSWD values of the secondary reference materials are around one

steps.action: Derived the RG2 age range (280–335 Ma, peak ~294 Ma, MSWD 10.6) and the QB-SZ age distribution (252–303 Ma peak plus 325–589 Ma oscillatory-zoned zircons), with trace-element ratios for each sample.
steps.quote: have a range of 280–335 Ma with a distinct peak at

steps.action: Interpreted the diffuse-contact enclave as a magmatic RG2 enclave (magma mingling) and the sharp-contact melanocratic enclaves as metasedimentary paragneiss xenoliths.
steps.quote: the sharp contact and the mineral paragenesis suggest an interpretation of these enclaves as xenoliths

steps.action: Compared QB-SZ mineralogy with the host granite, with published meta-lamprophyre mineralogy (always amphibole-bearing), and with the xenoliths.
steps.quote: the (meta-)lamprophyres, unlike the QB-SZ, always contain amphibole

steps.action: Proposed xenoliths as the source rocks of the QB-SZ, a rival to the sheared-lamprophyre interpretation.
steps.quote: Therefore, xenoliths in the Rotondo granite should be considered as source rocks of the QB-SZ.

steps.action: Stated two rival explanations for the fine-grained quartz domains (subgrain rotation under different conditions versus grain-size pinning by second phases) and favoured pinning from overlapping grain-size distributions in RG1.
steps.quote: For the occurrence of the finer-grained quartz domains, two interpretations are possible

steps.action: Inferred deformation temperatures from grain-boundary-migration microstructures (about 500–700 °C, with caveats on strain rate and water) and from rigid calcite in quartz veins.
steps.quote: indicating deformation under high-grade conditions at about 500–700 °C

steps.action: Compared the rough deformation temperatures with the compiled Alpine peak temperatures (~475–500 °C) along the tunnel.
steps.quote: may have occurred when Alpine peak temperature conditions prevailed

steps.action: Excluded D2 (kinematics and timing mismatch), D4 (shear zones pre-date strike-slip faults), earlier structures overturned by folding (would give unknown normal shear), and inherited rift normal faults (ductile character).
steps.quote: they do not fit to the ‘D2 stage’ nor the ‘D4 stage’ and thus are most probably related to the ‘D3 stage’

steps.action: Kept the attribution of the shear zones to south-verging backthrusting during the D3 stage, conditional on an Alpine age.
steps.quote: it is suggested that the backthrusts along the shear zones are a part of the scenario during the ‘D3 stage’ in the Gotthard massif

steps.action: Supported the published localization of brittle faults on ductile shear zones and proposed shifting the published 18–14 Ma timing of the strike-slip faults to younger ages.
steps.quote: it appears that the time estimate of Lützenkirchen and Loew (39) should be shifted toward younger ages

steps.action: Replaced mean ages with age ranges because of the high MSWD, then compared the RG1 and RG2 ranges: the RG1 range lies within the RG2 range.
steps.quote: which leads to the interpretation that both granite varieties are part of the same magmatic episode

steps.action: Supported the same-episode reading with KDE peaks (~295 and ~294 Ma), with the magma-mingling enclave, and with consistency with the published 294 ± 1.1 Ma age.
steps.quote: Furthermore, this interpretation is supported by the kernel density estimates (KDE, Vermeesch, 84) shown in Fig. 17

steps.action: Compared the proportion of pre-granite (>335 Ma) zircons in the QB-SZ (about one third) with the rare inherited cores in both granite samples.
steps.quote: In contrast, both granite samples contain only rare inherited cores.

steps.action: Rejected the published interpretation of the QB-SZ as sheared lamprophyres cogenetic with the granite.
steps.quote: [...] the interpretation that the QB-SZ are not sheared lamprophyres that are cogenetic with the host Rotondo granite, as previously thought

steps.action: Reinforced the xenolith reading with the independent mineralogical similarity of the xenoliths and the QB-SZ.
steps.quote: Numerous xenoliths within the Rotondo granite have a similar composition as the QB-SZ (Sect. 5.2), which reinforces this interpretation.

steps.action: Stated two rival explanations for the 252–303 Ma QB-SZ ages (post-emplacement fluid reset versus intrusion-related reset with Pb loss), leaned to the second, and left the question open; 207Pb/206Pb ages were too imprecise to decide.
steps.quote: Overall, it remains unclear what the meaning of the age range between 252 and 303 Ma in zircons from the QB-SZ is

steps.action: Concluded with the claims on D3 backthrusting, G-SZ localization at rheological contacts, the same magmatic episode for RG1 and RG2, and the QB-SZ as sheared xenoliths.
steps.quote: but rather that the QB-SZ are sheared xenoliths within the granite

tree.answer: Ductile shear zones (granitic and quartz-biotite-rich) in a nearly undeformed granite
Kinematics yes; protolith and ages no, need zircon U–Pb inference
Constrain shear-zone kinematics and timing, granite age, and QB-SZ protolith
Lamprophyre vs xenolith; D2/D3/D4 or inherited structures; SGR vs pinning
Yes: inherited zircon abundance and mineralogy separate lamprophyre from xenolith
Conditions found in tunnel exposures and traces
Partly: reference-material controls and independent lines, but one sample per lithology
QB-SZ sheared xenoliths; D3 backthrusting; RG1 and RG2 one episode

end.claim: The quartz-biotite-rich shear zones are not sheared lamprophyres cogenetic with the Rotondo granite, as previously thought, but strongly sheared basement paragneiss xenoliths, shown by about 30% pre-granite zircons and xenolith-like mineralogy.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the abundant >335 Ma zircons of the QB-SZ sample with the rare inherited cores in both granite samples is what turns the lamprophyre-versus-xenolith question into a rejection of the lamprophyre interpretation.

gates.evidence: Action: the zircon sampling of the QB-SZ was directed by the stated parent-material question (§4 ¶1), but the xenolith hypothesis is stated only in the Discussion, so it is not shown to have directed acquisition. Claim: the inheritance test could have failed (few old zircons would not discriminate against a cogenetic origin), and the lamprophyre rival was excluded; it rests on a single QB-SZ sample. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data; age ranges replaced mean ages after the MSWD was seen (§5.3 ¶2).

imports.item: High-voltage pulse fragmentation (SELFRAG) for rock disaggregation
Cathodoluminescence imaging on a scanning electron microscope
NIST-610 glass standard for trace-element calibration
Modified Chauvenet's criterion for outlier rejection
Mean squared weighted deviation (MSWD) as goodness of fit
Kernel density estimates of age distributions

novelty_claims.quote: No age determinations for the porphyritic Rotondo granite exist so far.
we focus on ductile shear zones in the Rotondo granite along the Bedretto tunnel, since less attention has been paid to them in previous studies
the separation of the two varieties by a QB-SZ in the SE was not reported
New geochronological U–Pb data show that both the equigranular and porphyritic varieties of the Rotondo granite formed during the same late-Variscan magmatic episode

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: D3 backthrusting is best_explanation and conditional on an Alpine age ('If it is assumed that the ductile shear zones developed during the Alpine orogenesis', §5.2.2 ¶2). RG1 and RG2 belonging to one magmatic episode is best_explanation; a precise intrusion age is explicitly not obtained (§5.3 ¶2), so there is no estimate_with_resolution. The deformation temperatures are rough estimates with stated caveats (§5.2.1 ¶3). The fine-grained quartz origin is left between two interpretations, and the meaning of the 252–303 Ma QB-SZ ages is no_conclusion (§5.4 ¶3). The age of the shear zones is not dated. Each lithology rests on one zircon sample (one QB-SZ, B20-2801), so replication across samples is absent. The paper is partly a review and site characterization for BULGG, and much structural data is adopted from Schneider (1985). Peer review is acknowledged (Michael Stipp and two anonymous reviewers) but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded and review-driven changes are unknown. Inference: the xenolith hypothesis may have emerged after the field and petrographic work rather than guiding the zircon sampling; the document does not say.

disagreements.target: [...] (1985); Lützenkirchen (2002); Lützenkirchen and Loew (2011): QB-SZ as sheared lamprophyres
disagreements.support: About one third of QB-SZ zircons are older than the granite age ranges while the granites have rare inherited cores, and the QB-SZ lack the amphibole of meta-lamprophyres and resemble the xenoliths.
disagreements.quote: [...] the interpretation that the QB-SZ are not sheared lamprophyres that are cogenetic with the host Rotondo granite, as previously thought

disagreements.target: Hafner (1958) and earlier studies: Rotondo granite nearly undeformed
disagreements.support: Tunnel mapping shows a weak foliation and centimeter- to meter-thick granitic and dark shear zones.
disagreements.quote: Previous studies suggested that the Rotondo granite is nearly undeformed (e.g. Hafner, 19).

disagreements.support: New mapping records the sharp RG2–RG1 contact in the NW and the QB-SZ separating the varieties in the SE, not reported before.
disagreements.quote: the separation of the two varieties by a QB-SZ in the SE was not reported

disagreements.target: Lützenkirchen and Loew (2011) timing of brittle strike-slip faults (18–14 Ma)
disagreements.support: Peak metamorphic temperatures at ~19–18 Ma and the timing of the Oberaar phase imply that the 200–300 °C faulting must be younger.
disagreements.quote: it appears that the time estimate of Lützenkirchen and Loew (39) should be shifted toward younger ages

disagreements.target: Sergeev et al. (1995) intrusion age of 294 ± 1.1 Ma
disagreements.support: The wide LA-ICP-MS age ranges with high MSWD, and the few zircons behind the ID-TIMS age, suggest it may be a mixed age rather than a distinct event.
disagreements.quote: raise the question of whether their age corresponds to a ‘distinct’ intrusion event or represents a mixed age of a range

disagreements.target: Sergeev and Steiger (1993): ~270 Ma zircons as post-intrusive recrystallization
disagreements.support: The new granite age ranges extend low enough that the ~270 Ma ages may be the lower end of the range rather than a distinct event.
disagreements.quote: the age data of the Rotondo granite samples show that their data may simply be at the lower end of the age range

alternatives_considered.chosen: Age ranges (and KDE peaks) for RG1 and RG2
alternatives_considered.reason: High MSWD indicates geological scatter, so a precise intrusion age cannot be calculated

alternatives_considered.alternatives: 207Pb/206Pb ages, which are not affected by Pb loss
alternatives_considered.reason: Uncertainties of the 207Pb/206Pb ages are too large

alternatives_considered.chosen: Grain size controlled by pinning by second phases (favoured)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Subgrain rotation recrystallization under different conditions
alternatives_considered.reason: Second phases are more common in fine-grained domains, subgrains are almost absent, and RG1 grain-size distributions overlap within one standard deviation

alternatives_considered.alternatives: D2 thrusting; D4 (Oberaar) strike-slip; earlier shear zones overturned by Basòdino-Cristallina folding; inherited rift normal faults
alternatives_considered.reason: Kinematics and timing mismatch D2; shear zones pre-date D4 faults; overturning would give an unknown normal shear sense; ductile character rules out rift faults

alternatives_considered.chosen: Reset related to the granite intrusion with increased Pb loss (leaned to, not decided)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Reset by late- to post-magmatic fluids after emplacement
alternatives_considered.reason: The large 252–303 Ma range shows a potential reset; the question remains open

alternatives_considered.chosen: White mica reflecting the peraluminous granite, with calcite from CO2-bearing metamorphic fluid
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Metasomatic weakening producing white mica and calcite
alternatives_considered.reason: White mica also occurs in undeformed granite, while calcite is restricted to the shear zones
